title: Syntax and data types
description: The stable Python foundations used throughout backend and AI engineering.
learning_objectives: Read and write basic Python statements
Choose and convert core scalar types
Explain Python's dynamic yet strong typing

sections.title: Python syntax basics
sections.markdown: Python uses newlines to separate most statements and indentation to define blocks. Comments begin with `#`. Consistent four-space indentation makes control flow visible and prevents syntax errors.

examples.explanation: The indented line belongs to the if block.

sections.title: Variables and assignment
sections.markdown: Assignment binds a name to an object. A variable is a name, not a typed storage box. Reassignment makes the name refer to another object; it does not mutate the previous object.

examples.explanation: The name is rebound to the computed integer.

sections.title: Naming rules
sections.markdown: Identifiers may contain letters, digits, and underscores, but cannot start with a digit or use a Python keyword. Prefer descriptive `snake_case` names for variables and functions.

sections.title: Integers
sections.markdown: `int` represents whole numbers with arbitrary precision in normal Python. Operators include `+`, `-`, `*`, `//`, `%`, and `**`. `/` produces a float even when operands are integers.

examples.explanation: Floor division, remainder, and true division have different results.

sections.title: Floating-point numbers
sections.learning_objective: Use floats while recognizing precision limits.
sections.markdown: `float` represents binary floating-point values. Many decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly, so compare calculated floats with a tolerance rather than exact equality when precision matters.

examples.explanation: Rounding is useful for display; domain-specific precision may require Decimal.

sections.title: Strings
sections.markdown: `str` stores immutable Unicode text. Use quotes to create strings, indexing and slicing to read characters, and f-strings to format values. String methods return new strings rather than changing the original.

examples.explanation: upper returns a new string and the f-string embeds it.

sections.title: Booleans
sections.markdown: `bool` has exactly two values: `True` and `False`. Comparisons produce booleans. `and`, `or`, and `not` combine conditions; remember that `and` and `or` return operands, not necessarily literal booleans.

sections.title: None
sections.markdown: `None` is the singleton used for no value or not yet available. Compare it with `is None`, not `== None`. A function with no explicit return statement returns `None`.

examples.explanation: Identity comparison is the idiomatic check.

sections.title: Dynamic and strong typing
sections.markdown: Python is dynamically typed because names can be rebound to objects of different types at runtime. It is strongly typed because incompatible operations generally fail instead of silently coercing unrelated values.

examples.explanation: Rebinding is allowed, but incompatible addition is rejected.

sections.title: Inspecting with type()
sections.markdown: `type(value)` returns the concrete runtime type. It is useful while learning and debugging. Production branching often prefers `isinstance(value, ExpectedType)` because it accounts for subclasses.

sections.title: Type conversion and casting
sections.markdown: Constructors such as `int()`, `float()`, `str()`, and `bool()` perform explicit conversions. Invalid text raises `ValueError`, so validate or handle exceptions at input boundaries. `bool('False')` is True because a non-empty string is truthy.

examples.explanation: External text is converted at the boundary.

sections.title: Mutable and immutable awareness
sections.markdown: Core scalars such as integers, floats, strings, booleans, and None are immutable. Operations create new objects. Mutable containers such as lists can change in place, which matters when aliases or function arguments share the same object.
key_points: Shared mutable objects can change through aliases

sections.title: Common type-related mistakes
sections.markdown: Frequent mistakes include mixing strings and numbers, relying on truthiness when `0` is meaningful, using `== None`, shadowing built-ins such as `str`, and assuming float arithmetic is exact. Convert and validate data at system boundaries.

sections.title: Interview-focused summary
sections.markdown: In an interview, state that Python is dynamically and strongly typed, explain that variables bind names to objects, distinguish immutable scalars from mutable containers, and show explicit conversion with error handling. Use precise examples rather than memorized labels.

summary: Python names bind to typed objects.
Core scalar types include int, float, str, bool, and None.
Explicit conversion and boundary validation prevent common failures.
interview_takeaways: Python is dynamically and strongly typed.
Rebinding differs from mutating an object.
common_mistakes: Assuming reading a value proves mastery
